newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Lee, Tung vie for U.S. support.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Lee, Tung vie for U.S. support.

text.p: Hong Kong's future chief Tung Chee-hwa and democracy movement leader Martin Lee are vying for U.S. support as the territory heads towards reunification with China on July 1, political analysts said on Monday.
Lee is in Washington lobbying against Beijing's plans to curb civil and political liberties in Hong Kong after July 1 and has secured a meeting with President Bill Clinton ahead of Tung.
Lee will see Clinton, Vice President Al Gore and Secretary of State Madeleine Albright this week.

Tung, chosen by a China-controlled caucus in December, has planned his own official trip to Washington before Britain hands Hong Kong back to China, but details have not yet been finalised, his office said.
"Martin Lee wants U.S. support on Hong Kong issues as British influence is declining. He wants to get support, recognition, even affection from the U.S.," political analyst Sonny Lo told Reuters.
"Tung, on the other hand, needs to counterbalance Lee," said Lo, who is making a long-term study on the sovereignty change.
Pro-China politician and academic, Lau Siu-kai, said Lee had upstaged the future leader.
"He has pre-empted Tung to a certain extent. Tung will have a hard time with the press and with Congress," Lau told Reuters.
Lau said both Lee and Tung had strong reasons to court the United States.
"As his influence is declining in Hong Kong, it will be difficult for Lee to mobilise opposition against China or the future Hong Kong government. He needs support from the U.S.," Lau said.
"Tung wants to help modernise China. As the West still holds the economic might, he needs U.S. goodwill," he said.
Hong Kong, a British colony for more than 150 years, reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 under the terms of a 1984 Sino-British handover treaty.
The treaty promises the territory's 6.4 million people that they can keep their capitalist way of life and a large degree of autonomy for 50 years after the change of flag.

Despite the treaty, Beijing has launched plans to dismantle the territory's elected legislature and replace it with the China-anointed Provisional Legislature, and has started moves to change civil liberties laws, including the Bill of Rights.
Tung last week proposed to curb the public's right to protest and foreign funding of political groups from July 1.

Britain and the U.S. have criticised these moves, and pro-democracy activists have accused China of breaking its vows. Tung's popularity has dipped in recent days over his support for curbs on civil liberties, opinion polls showed on Monday.
Hong Kong Baptist University political scientist Michael DeGolyer said Lee's meeting with Clinton might embarrass Tung.
DeGolyer also warned that China's planned clampdown on civil liberties in Hong Kong had parallels with the McCarthyite political witch-hunts of the United States in the 1950s.
He said justifying a rollback on civil liberties on grounds of "national security", as Hong Kong's future government did last week, opened the door wide in the interpretation of crimes.
"This question of national security is a critical one," he said. "Anyone who can recall the MacCarthy era in the United States knows 'national security' can cover a multitude of sins."
The late U.S. senator Joe McCarthy led political witch-hunts in the United States in the late 1940s and 1950s in which people seen as leftists were labeled "reds" or communist spies.
